↑ Back to top

Chapter 3

Disk Subsystem Performance

How SQL Server talks to disk, how to read I/O latency per file, why your SAN dashboard can look perfect while queries crawl — and how checkpoint tuning fixes the most common burst problem.

Book pages 45–67 · 8 figures · 3 code listings

1Why I/O is still the problem

SQL Server is relentlessly I/O-intensive — always reading and writing. Good I/O throughput is essential to health. And critically: many installations are still I/O bound even on modern flash storage. Faster disks don't automatically fix a workload that asks them for too much.

The plan for this chapter

First, how SQL Server processes I/O internally (it's more subtle than "read the page"). Then how to measure it at every layer of the stack — SQL Server, OS, virtualization, storage. Then checkpoint tuning, the most common cause of I/O bursts. Finally, the five I/O waits you'll actually see.

2Anatomy of the I/O subsystem

FoundationSQL Server never touches a data page on disk

This is the key mental model. Every time a page is read or modified, SQL Server pulls it into memory and caches it in the buffer pool. Each page there is referenced by a buffer structure containing:

  • The page's address in the data file
  • A pointer to the data page in memory
  • Status information
  • The page's latching queue

Latches protect these in-memory structures from corruption when multiple threads touch them. Two common types: exclusive (blocks all access) and shared (allows concurrent reads, blocks modification). Conceptually they're like critical sections or mutexes in application code — Chapter 10 covers them properly.

Logical vs. physical reads

A logical read happens every single time SQL Server accesses a page in the buffer pool. A physical read happens only when the page isn't in memory and must be fetched from disk. Buffer pool pages are not stored in file order — SQL Server can still find any page instantly.

When data changes, SQL Server writes log records to the transaction log, then modifies the page in the buffer pool and marks it dirty. Dirty pages are saved to the data files asynchronously by the checkpoint process and sometimes by lazy writer. Importantly: a modification still requires reading the page from disk first if it isn't already cached.

SchedulingWhy I/O must be asynchronous

Remember from Chapter 2: cooperative scheduling, workers yielding every 4 ms. That model cannot tolerate a worker sitting still waiting for a disk, because the other workers would be blocked from running.

So SQL Server uses asynchronous I/O wherever possible. By default all schedulers handle I/O requests; the affinity I/O mask can bind I/O to specific CPUs, which in theory helps very busy OLTP systems — but the author rarely finds it necessary. Optimizations and load reduction work better.

Each scheduler has a dedicated I/O queue. A worker needing I/O creates a request structure, adds it to the queue, and fires an asynchronous OS API call. It then either keeps running or suspends itself into the SUSPENDED queue. When a new worker starts running on that scheduler, it walks the I/O queue, checks whether each OS call has finished, and calls the callback function to complete the request.

Three things to remember

1. All active schedulers handle I/O by default. 2. Most I/O uses asynchronous OS API calls — even write-ahead logging, where the worker issuing COMMIT may suspend until the log record hits disk, but the OS write itself is asynchronous. 3. The I/O request may be completed by a different worker than the one that issued it.

You can see pending requests in sys.dm_io_pending_io_requests. Two columns matter: io_pending_ms_ticks (how long it's been pending) and io_pending — which tells you whether the OS call has finished and the request is just waiting for a worker to pick it up. That distinction is how you tell whether latency is really disk-bound or actually CPU-starved.

Step by stepReading a data page

SQL Server checks the buffer pool. On a miss, this sequence runs:

  1. The worker allocates a buffer and protects it with an exclusive latch — blocking other workers from touching the page until it's read.
  2. It creates the I/O request structure, puts it in the scheduler's I/O queue, and issues the async OS read.
  3. It then tries to take a shared latch on the same buffer — which is immediately blocked by its own exclusive latch.
  4. The worker suspends with a PAGEIOLATCH wait.

Then another worker reaches a RUNNING state, checks the queue, finds the completed request, and calls the callback function. That function validates the page isn't corrupted and releases the exclusive latch. The original worker can now resume and read the page.

CriticalThe four errors you must alert on

ErrorMeaningWhat it usually means
823The OS I/O API call failedOften a hardware problem
605 / 824Logical consistency problems with data pagesRun DBCC CHECKDB immediately — could be corruption, or faulty I/O drivers corrupting pages in transit
833An I/O request took longer than 15 secondsAbnormal. Check disk subsystem health.
825An I/O request failed and had to be retriedCheck disk subsystem health.

All are severe — set up alerts for them. Investigate using the error log (Listing 1-4 from Chapter 1) and the system event log.

Good newsOne request, many pages

SQL Server often reads several pages per I/O request, so a query can log thousands of logical reads with only a handful of physical reads. Two mechanisms: read-ahead during scans, and ramp-up reads, which grab large batches of pages to fill the buffer pool quickly at startup.

WritesSimilar, but with a twist

Writes follow the same async pattern with different callbacks. The twist is durability: a transaction is not committed until log records are hardened on disk. Technically WAL looks like a synchronous write, but SQL Server still uses an asynchronous I/O pattern for it.

  • Checkpoint finds dirty pages in the buffer pool and writes them out, minimizing requests by combining adjacent modified pages into one operation.
  • Lazy writer sweeps the buffer pool to evict cold pages. Normally it skips dirty pages, but under memory pressure it will write them out.
  • Exception: bulk import allocates a reusable set of buffers and writes outside the checkpoint, so a massive import doesn't flush your entire buffer pool.

3The storage subsystem: a holistic view

This is where the author describes the most common political argument in IT. Database engineers say "the disks are slow." Storage engineers point at submillisecond SAN latency and say "the problem is on the SQL Server side."

Neither team is right

Both make the same mistake: reducing the storage subsystem to one or two components. Bad I/O performance can originate in any layer — so you have to analyze the whole stack.

There's also direct-attached storage (DAS) — NVMe drives installed locally or attached directly. It removes the network from the storage path and can deliver better I/O, at the cost of flexibility: no transparent capacity expansion or maintenance.

The key conceptThe tipping point

Every storage subsystem has a point past which latency grows exponentially as throughput rises. Before it, things are flat and pleasant:

IOPS workloadResponse time
1,0001 ms
50,0003 ms
100,000 (past the tipping point)double- or triple-digit ms

Every component has its own tipping point. Example: low queue depth in the HBA adapter causes queueing at the controller as requests pile up. SQL Server suffers terrible latency and performance — while every SAN metric stays perfectly healthy with no latency at all. That is exactly how the two teams end up shouting at each other.

Use the DiskSpd utility (on GitHub) to test the storage subsystem by emulating SQL Server's workload.

Start heresys.dm_io_virtual_file_stats

The single most important tool in SQL Server I/O troubleshooting. It gives per-database-file I/O statistics: operation counts, bytes read and written, and stalls (the time for I/O requests to complete). The book uses "stalls" and "latency" interchangeably.

The data is cumulative since restart, so you take two snapshots and compute the delta. Listing 3-1 does this and filters out files with low I/O activity, whose metrics are skewed and useless.

Listing 3-1 — Using the sys.dm_io_virtual_file_stats viewT-SQL
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS #Snapshot;
GO
CREATE TABLE #Snapshot
(
    database_id SMALLINT NOT NULL,
    file_id SMALLINT NOT NULL,
    num_of_reads BIGINT NOT NULL,
    num_of_bytes_read BIGINT NOT NULL,
    io_stall_read_ms BIGINT NOT NULL,
    num_of_writes BIGINT NOT NULL,
    num_of_bytes_written BIGINT NOT NULL,
    io_stall_write_ms BIGINT NOT NULL
);
INSERT INTO #Snapshot(database_id,file_id,num_of_reads,num_of_bytes_read
    ,io_stall_read_ms,num_of_writes,num_of_bytes_written,io_stall_write_ms)
    SELECT database_id,file_id,num_of_reads,num_of_bytes_read
        ,io_stall_read_ms,num_of_writes,num_of_bytes_written,io_stall_write_ms
    FROM sys.dm_io_virtual_file_stats(NULL,NULL)
OPTION (RECOMPILE);

-- Set test interval (1 minute).
WAITFOR DELAY '00:01:00.000';

;WITH Stats(db_id, file_id, Reads, ReadBytes, Writes
    ,WrittenBytes, ReadStall, WriteStall)
as
(
    SELECT
        s.database_id, s.file_id
        ,fs.num_of_reads - s.num_of_reads
        ,fs.num_of_bytes_read - s.num_of_bytes_read
        ,fs.num_of_writes - s.num_of_writes
        ,fs.num_of_bytes_written - s.num_of_bytes_written
        ,fs.io_stall_read_ms - s.io_stall_read_ms
        ,fs.io_stall_write_ms - s.io_stall_write_ms
    FROM
        #Snapshot s JOIN sys.dm_io_virtual_file_stats(NULL, NULL) fs ON
            s.database_id = fs.database_id and s.file_id = fs.file_id
)
SELECT
    s.db_id AS [DB ID], d.name AS [Database]
    ,mf.name AS [File Name], mf.physical_name AS [File Path]
    ,mf.type_desc AS [Type], s.Reads
    ,CONVERT(DECIMAL(12,3), s.ReadBytes / 1048576.) AS [Read MB]
    ,CONVERT(DECIMAL(12,3), s.WrittenBytes / 1048576.) AS [Written MB]
    ,s.Writes, s.Reads + s.Writes AS [IO Count]
    ,CONVERT(DECIMAL(5,2),100.0 * s.ReadBytes /
            (s.ReadBytes + s.WrittenBytes)) AS [Read %]
    ,CONVERT(DECIMAL(5,2),100.0 * s.WrittenBytes /
            (s.ReadBytes + s.WrittenBytes)) AS [Write %]
    ,s.ReadStall AS [Read Stall]
    ,s.WriteStall AS [Write Stall]
    ,CASE WHEN s.Reads = 0
        THEN 0.000
        ELSE CONVERT(DECIMAL(12,3),1.0 * s.ReadStall / s.Reads)
    END AS [Avg Read Stall]
    ,CASE WHEN s.Writes = 0
        THEN 0.000
        ELSE CONVERT(DECIMAL(12,3),1.0 * s.WriteStall / s.Writes)
    END AS [Avg Write Stall]
FROM
    Stats s JOIN sys.master_files mf WITH (NOLOCK) ON
        s.db_id = mf.database_id and
        s.file_id = mf.file_id
    JOIN sys.databases d WITH (NOLOCK) ON
        s.db_id = d.database_id
WHERE -- Only display files with more than 20MB throughput
    (s.ReadBytes + s.WrittenBytes) > 20 * 1048576
ORDER BY
    s.db_id, s.file_id
OPTION (RECOMPILE);

ThresholdsWhat latency is acceptable?

No universal thresholds exist, but these rules of thumb hold:

File typeNetwork storageDirect-attached
Transaction log writes1–2 mssub-millisecond
Data file reads & writes3–5 mssub-millisecond

Then analyze throughput. The diagnostic pairing is powerful:

  • High stalls with low throughput → the problem is almost certainly outside SQL Server (the storage path).
  • High stalls with high throughput → you may just be at or past the tipping point; check whether the volume is legitimate.
  • Remember to look at throughput across all files sharing the same drive or controller — one busy file raises latency for its neighbours.

Diagnosis by patternReading the symptom

What you seeWhat it usually meansWhere to go
Many reads + read stalls in data files, plus lots of PAGEIOLATCH waits and low Page Life ExpectancyLarge amounts of data constantly read from disk — usually nonoptimized queries doing big scansChapter 4. (Also consider plain under-provisioned memory.)
Many writes + write stalls in user database data filesOften an inefficient checkpoint configurationTune checkpoint (below). Longer term: drop unused indexes, fix FILLFACTOR to reduce page splits, add data compression, refactor schema.
Large throughput + stalls in tempdbVersion store activity, massive spills, or excessive temp object usageChapter 9
High resource wait time in PAGEIOLATCH and other I/O waitsSystem-wide I/O latency (no per-file detail)Use alongside the per-file view

LimitationThe view averages — counters show the spikes

sys.dm_io_virtual_file_stats averages over your sampling interval. That's fine when latency is low. When it's high, you need to know: is it consistently slow, or is it a few violent bursts? That calls for performance counters sampled finely alongside the SQL Server metrics.

On Windows, PerfMon is the simplest tool. Start with Avg Disk sec/Read, Avg Disk sec/Write, and Avg Disk Queue Length; if they spike, add SQL Server counters to find which process caused the burst.

ObjectCountersWhy you care
Physical DiskAvg Disk [Read/Write] Queue Length, Current Disk Queue LengthRequests queued at the OS level. Keep low; spikes = queueing.
Avg Disk sec/Transfer, .../Read, .../WriteLatency per interval — reveals whether stalls were constant or bursty
Disk Transfers/sec, Disk Reads/sec, Disk Writes/sec, Disk Bytes/sec, Avg Disk Bytes/TransferThroughput and I/O size — shows the shape of the workload
SQL Server: Buffer ManagerCheckpoint pages/sec, Background writer pages/secDirty pages written by checkpoint (the usual burst suspect)
Lazy writer/secPages written by lazy writer
Page reads/sec, Page writes/sec, Readahead pages/secPhysical I/O volume, including read-ahead
SQL Server: DatabasesLog Bytes Flushed/sec, Log Flush Write Time (ms), Log Flushes/sec, Transactions/secLog throughput, latency and request count — use these to see whether log generation is uniform
SQL Server: SQL StatisticsBatch Requests/secNot I/O itself, but exposes workload spikes that cause I/O bursts
Don't forget the other tenants

Check what other applications run on that server. An antivirus scan or backup agent can be responsible for the I/O bursts you're chasing.

On Linux there's no PerfMon, but iostat, dstat, and iotop ship with most distributions and give per-process or system-level disk metrics.

From inside SQL Server, read the same counters through sys.dm_os_performance_counters. Listing 3-2 samples every second and computes rates for the per-second counters. On a named instance, change the SQLServer prefix in object_name to MSSQL$YOUR_INSTANCE_NAME.

Listing 3-2 — Using the sys.dm_os_performance_counters viewT-SQL
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS #PerfCntrs;
GO
CREATE TABLE #PerfCntrs
(
    collected_time DATETIME2(7) NOT NULL DEFAULT SYSDATETIME(),
    object_name SYSNAME NOT NULL,
    counter_name SYSNAME NOT NULL,
    instance_name SYSNAME NOT NULL,
    cntr_value BIGINT NOT NULL,
    PRIMARY KEY (object_name, counter_name, instance_name)
);
;WITH Counters(obj_name, ctr_name)
AS
(
    SELECT C.obj_name, C.ctr_name
    FROM
    (
        VALUES
            ('SQLServer:Buffer Manager','Checkpoint pages/sec')
            ,('SQLServer:Buffer Manager','Background writer pages/sec')
            ,('SQLServer:Buffer Manager','Lazy writes/sec')
            ,('SQLServer:Buffer Manager','Page reads/sec')
            ,('SQLServer:Buffer Manager','Page writes/sec')
            ,('SQLServer:Buffer Manager','Readahead pages/sec')
            ,('SQLServer:Databases','Log Flushes/sec') -- For all DBs
            ,('SQLServer:Databases','Log Bytes Flushed/sec') -- For all DBs
            ,('SQLServer:Databases','Log Flush Write Time (ms)') -- For all DBs
            ,('SQLServer:Databases','Transactions/sec') -- For all DBs
            ,('SQLServer:SQL Statistics','Batch Requests/sec')
    ) C(obj_name, ctr_name)
)
INSERT INTO #PerfCntrs(object_name,counter_name,instance_name,cntr_value)
    SELECT
        pc.object_name, pc.counter_name, pc.instance_name, pc.cntr_value
    FROM
        sys.dm_os_performance_counters pc WITH (NOLOCK) JOIN Counters c ON
            pc.counter_name = c.ctr_name AND pc.object_name = c.obj_name;

WAITFOR DELAY '00:00:01.000';

;WITH Counters(obj_name, ctr_name)
AS
(
    SELECT C.obj_name, C.ctr_name
    FROM
    (
        VALUES
            ('SQLServer:Buffer Manager','Checkpoint pages/sec')
            ,('SQLServer:Buffer Manager','Background writer pages/sec')
            ,('SQLServer:Buffer Manager','Lazy writes/sec')
            ,('SQLServer:Buffer Manager','Page reads/sec')
            ,('SQLServer:Buffer Manager','Page writes/sec')
            ,('SQLServer:Buffer Manager','Readahead pages/sec')
            ,('SQLServer:Databases','Log Flushes/sec') -- For all DBs
            ,('SQLServer:Databases','Log Bytes Flushed/sec') -- For all DBs
            ,('SQLServer:Databases','Log Flush Write Time (ms)') -- For all DBs
            ,('SQLServer:Databases','Transactions/sec') -- For all DBs
            ,('SQLServer:SQL Statistics','Batch Requests/sec')
    ) C(obj_name, ctr_name)
)
SELECT
    pc.object_name, pc.counter_name, pc.instance_name
    ,CASE pc.cntr_type
        WHEN 272696576 THEN
            (pc.cntr_value - h.cntr_value) * 1000 /
                DATEDIFF(MILLISECOND,h.collected_time,SYSDATETIME())
        WHEN 65792 THEN
            pc.cntr_value
        ELSE NULL
    END as cntr_value
FROM
    sys.dm_os_performance_counters pc WITH (NOLOCK) JOIN Counters c ON
        pc.counter_name = c.ctr_name AND pc.object_name = c.obj_name
    JOIN #PerfCntrs h ON
        pc.object_name = h.object_name AND
        pc.counter_name = h.counter_name AND
        pc.instance_name = h.instance_name
ORDER BY
    pc.object_name, pc.counter_name, pc.instance_name
OPTION (RECOMPILE);

Deeper layersVirtualization, HBA, and the array

Beyond the OS, three more layers can be the culprit: virtualization, the HBA/SCSI controller, and the storage array itself.

First, if virtualized, confirm the host isn't overcommitted — that alone causes every kind of performance problem.

Then, unless you're on local storage, I/O requests are serialized and sent over a network, and there are two classic problems:

ProblemSymptomFix
Insufficient queue depth somewhere in the I/O pathLow latency on storage but much higher latency in the VM/OS, with disk queueing presentIncrease queue depth in datastore, vSCSI controller, and HBA settings
Noisy neighboursMultiple I/O-intensive VMs on one host, or many high-throughput servers sharing network and storage, degrading each otherHard. Requires analysing multiple infrastructure components.
Careful with queue depth

Storage arrays have a limit on outstanding requests. Raising queue depth on a busy server pushes more requests at the array — you may simply shift the bottleneck from one layer to another, especially if the array serves many busy systems.

Both the virtualization host and the storage expose throughput, IOPS, and latency metrics. Hyper-V lets you use regular disk counters on the host; VMware gives you ESXTOP (Chapter 15). The approach never changes: collect, correlate, find the bottleneck.

ConfigurationAlignment actually matters

Use the storage vendor's published SQL Server best practices as a starting point — but pay real attention to alignment between allocation unit size, RAID stripe size, and partition offset.

ConfigurationResult
1024 MB partition offset · 4 KB disk block · 64 KB allocation unit · 128 KB RAID stripe✅ Perfectly aligned — each I/O request served by a single disk
Same, but 96 KB RAID stripes❌ Each 64 KB allocation unit spans two disks — extra I/O requests, serious performance impact

Work with your infrastructure and storage engineers — they're the subject matter experts and will find the root cause faster. And for predictable performance in critical systems, the best answer is a dedicated environment: dedicated hardware with DAS.

4Checkpoint tuning

SQL Server uses write-ahead logging: transactions commit once log records are hardened, and dirty pages can be written later because the changes can be replayed from the log.

The checkpoint's job is to save data pages into the data files. Its real purpose is recovery time: fewer un-replayed changes means faster recovery after a crash or failover. The maximum desired recovery time is set at server or database level, both defaulting to 60 seconds.

Don't treat it as a contract

The recovery target is not a hard value. Databases often recover far faster. And bursts of activity plus long-running transactions can push recovery beyond the target.

Four kindsKnow which one is running

TypeTriggerBehaviour
InternalStarted by operations like beginning a backup or creating a database snapshotAutomatic, tied to that operation
ManualYou run CHECKPOINTOn demand
AutomaticThe historical default; recovery interval set server-wideWakes once or a few times per interval and flushes dirty pages — causes write bursts, painful on busy systems
Indirect (2012+)Per-databaseRuns far more frequently, sometimes continuously, balancing the I/O load. Use this whenever possible.
The upgrade trap

Indirect checkpoint is on by default only for databases created in SQL Server 2016 or later. It is not enabled automatically when you upgrade an instance, and it isn't on in 2012/2014. Databases carried forward from older versions keep the old automatic checkpoint — even on a shiny new SQL Server 2016 install. Enable it per database with ALTER DATABASE ... SET TARGET_RECOVERY_TIME.

Enabling an indirect checkpoint per databaseT-SQL
-- 90 seconds is a good starting point in many busy OLTP systems.
ALTER DATABASE [YourDatabase]
    SET TARGET_RECOVERY_TIME = 90 SECONDS WITH NO_WAIT;
GO

-- Verify what each database is using (0 = automatic checkpoint).
SELECT name, target_recovery_time_in_seconds
FROM sys.databases
ORDER BY name;

Case studyThe 60-second average that hid a 1-second disaster

A real system showed very high write latency in a 1-minute sample from sys.dm_io_virtual_file_stats. But 1–3 second samples rarely showed any activity at all. That discrepancy is the signature of a burst.

The author then confirmed the hypothesis with Checkpoint pages/sec, Disk Writes/sec, and Avg Disk Queue Length — that's the PerfMon screenshot in Figure 3-5 above, showing the burst clearly.

Although the instance ran SQL Server 2016, it was using automatic checkpoint, because every database had been upgraded from an earlier version — exactly the trap described above. Enabling indirect checkpoint changed the I/O pattern immediately.

Indirect checkpoints don't eliminate bursts entirely — spikes in data modification can still produce them, just far less often than with automatic checkpoints. You may also need to tune the recovery target for the most balanced I/O: in this case 90 seconds gave the best result. Remember that higher values increase recovery time.

5The five I/O waits

When the disk subsystem isn't fast enough, it's very common to see all of these present at once. Learn to tell them apart — each points somewhere different.

Wait 1ASYNC_IO_COMPLETION

Waiting for asynchronous I/O on pages other than buffer pool pages. Common sources:

  • Regular checkpoint
  • Internal checkpoint when starting a backup or running DBCC CHECKDB
  • Reading GAM pages from data files
  • Reading data pages during a database backup — which unfortunately skews the average wait time, making it harder to analyse

How to react: if it appears alongside PAGEIOLATCH, do general I/O troubleshooting. If PAGEIOLATCH is absent, check how often it occurs — and you may ignore it when its percentage is low and disk latency is fine.

Wait 2IO_COMPLETION

Occurs during synchronous reads and writes in data files, and some transaction log reads. Examples:

  • Reading allocation map pages
  • Reading the transaction log during database recovery
  • Writing data to tempdb during sort spills

How to react: general disk troubleshooting — but pay specific attention to tempdb latency and throughput. In the author's experience, bad tempdb performance is the most common cause of this wait (Chapter 9).

Wait 3WRITELOG

Waiting for log records to be written to the transaction log. Seeing it is normal in any system; a large percentage suggests a real log bottleneck. Check both the average wait time and the transaction log write latency in sys.dm_io_virtual_file_stats — high values there are impactful and can affect overall throughput. Chapter 11 covers the remedies.

Wait 4WRITE_COMPLETION

Synchronous writes to database and log files. In the author's experience it's most common with database snapshots: SQL Server persists the pre-snapshot versions of pages, so at a checkpoint it reads old page copies and writes them to the snapshot before writing dirty pages to disk. That can greatly increase total I/O.

How to react: check whether snapshots exist — and remember some internal processes, like DBCC CHECKDB, create internal snapshots too. If snapshots are legitimate, improve disk performance to support them; if not, remove them.

Wait 5PAGEIOLATCH

The wait for data pages being read from disk into the buffer pool — universal, present in every system. There are technically six variants, but only three are noticeable:

VariantWhen it fires
PAGEIOLATCH_EXWorker wants to update the page and waits for it to be read from disk
PAGEIOLATCH_SHWorker wants to read the page and waits for it to be read from disk
PAGEIOLATCH_UPWorker wants to update a system page (e.g. an allocation map) and waits for it to be read

Excessive PAGEIOLATCH means SQL Server is constantly reading from disk. Two causes:

  1. Under-provisioned memory — the active data set doesn't fit in the buffer pool.
  2. More common: nonoptimized queries scanning unnecessary data and flushing the buffer pool.

Cross-check with Page Life Expectancy (PLE) — how long pages stay in the buffer pool. Baseline rule of thumb: 300 seconds per 4 GB of buffer pool, so a 100 GB buffer pool should sit around 7,500 seconds.

Listing 3-3 — Getting Page Life Expectancy in the systemT-SQL
SELECT object_name, counter_name, instance_name, cntr_value as [PLE(sec)]
FROM sys.dm_os_performance_counters WITH (NOLOCK)
WHERE counter_name = 'Page life expectancy'
OPTION (RECOMPILE);

This returns a value per NUMA node, so in a multi-node system you get several rows — check them individually, since one node can be starved while another looks fine.

A large percentage of PAGEIOLATCH waits always needs attention. It may not be customer-facing yet, especially on low-latency flash arrays — but data growth will eventually push the disk subsystem past its limit, and then it affects everything at once.

Ranked solutions

You can reduce PAGEIOLATCH by upgrading disks or adding memory. But the best approach is to reduce the amount of data read from disk — find and optimize the inefficient queries. That's Chapter 4.

6Key takeaways

  • SQL Server uses cooperative scheduling and, mostly, asynchronous I/O. Each scheduler has its own I/O queue and handles I/O by default.
  • sys.dm_io_virtual_file_stats gives throughput and latency per database file. Targets: log writes 1–2 ms; data file reads and writes 3–5 ms on network storage, lower on DAS.
  • Analyse the whole I/O stack. The problem may be in the OS, virtualization, network path, queue depth, or the array — a healthy SAN KPI proves nothing about the layers above it.
  • High latency is often caused by bursts, not sustained load. Use performance counters to see the shape, not just the average.
  • Tune the checkpoint. Automatic checkpoint is one of the most common offenders in busy systems; indirect checkpoint usually fixes it for free.
  • Reducing disk activity through query optimization is one of the best ways to improve latency overall.
What's next

Chapter 4 turns to inefficient queries — the single largest source of unnecessary I/O, and the fix that costs nothing in hardware.

↑ Back to top

Chapter 4

Inefficient Queries

The bad queries that pay off Chapter 3's debts — how they hurt you, and the four ways to hunt them down: the plan cache, xEvents, the Query Store, and third-party tools.

Book pages 69–103 · 9 figures · 10 code listings

1The impact of inefficient queries

Inefficient queries exist in every system. The author's blunt assessment: he has yet to see a system that wouldn't benefit from query optimization. Healthy systems are rare — and only because nobody calls a consultant in to admire one.

Why it gets postponedThe honest economics

Not every company prioritises query tuning, and that's a rational choice for a while. Tuning is time-consuming and tedious, and shipping faster is often worth more than saving CPU cycles. So teams throw hardware at the problem instead.

That works — until it doesn't. Poorly optimized queries hurt from three directions at once:

DamageMechanismWhy hardware stops helping
Disk (most obvious)Large scans overload the I/O subsystem, so the whole system suffersYou can add memory to grow the buffer pool and cut physical I/O — but as data grows it becomes impractical, and non-Enterprise editions cap buffer pool size
CPUEvery extra logical read and in-memory page scan burns CPU. Microseconds each — but they add up fastMore CPUs means more licences, non-Enterprise editions cap CPU count, and it still doesn't fix blocking
BlockingBad queries hold locks longer, so other sessions waitYou can reduce blocking without tuning, but that changes system behaviour and has its own performance cost
The working rule

Always analyse whether queries are poorly optimized, then estimate their impact. Practically: tune queries when you see high disk throughput, blocking, or high CPU. If the data is fully cached and CPU looks acceptable, you may reasonably focus elsewhere first — but keep data growth in mind, because the day the active set outgrows the buffer pool, the impact arrives suddenly and severely.

The good news

Query optimization is not all-or-nothing. Optimizing just a handful of frequently executed queries can produce dramatic improvements. So the entire game is detection — which is what the rest of the chapter is about.

2Plan cache–based execution statistics

SQL Server caches and reuses execution plans, and for each cached plan it maintains execution statistics: how many times it ran, cumulative CPU time, I/O load. That's a ready-made list of your most expensive queries.

It isn't the most comprehensive technique — it has real limitations — but it's very easy, works in every SQL Server version, and requires no monitoring setup at all. The data is already there. That makes it the right first move.

Listing 4-1 — Using the sys.dm_exec_query_stats viewT-SQL
;WITH Queries
AS
(
    SELECT TOP 50
       qs.creation_time AS [Cached Time]
       ,qs.last_execution_time AS [Last Exec Time]
       ,qs.execution_count AS [Exec Cnt]
       ,CONVERT(DECIMAL(10,5),
            IIF
            (
                DATEDIFF(SECOND,qs.creation_time, qs.last_execution_time) = 0
                ,NULL
                ,1.0 * qs.execution_count /
                    DATEDIFF(SECOND,qs.creation_time, qs.last_execution_time)
            )
        ) AS [Exec Per Second]
        ,(qs.total_logical_reads + qs.total_logical_writes) /
            qs.execution_count AS [Avg IO]
        ,(qs.total_worker_time / qs.execution_count / 1000)
            AS [Avg CPU(ms)]
        ,qs.total_logical_reads AS [Total Reads]
        ,qs.last_logical_reads AS [Last Reads]
        ,qs.total_logical_writes AS [Total Writes]
        ,qs.last_logical_writes AS [Last Writes]
        ,qs.total_worker_time / 1000 AS [Total Worker Time]
        ,qs.last_worker_time / 1000 AS [Last Worker Time]
        ,qs.total_elapsed_time / 1000 AS [Total Elapsed Time]
        ,qs.last_elapsed_time / 1000 AS [Last Elapsed Time]
        ,qs.total_rows AS [Total Rows]
        ,qs.last_rows AS [Last Rows]
        ,qs.total_rows / qs.execution_count AS [Avg Rows]
        ,qs.total_physical_reads AS [Total Physical Reads]
        ,qs.last_physical_reads AS [Last Physical Reads]
        ,qs.total_physical_reads / qs.execution_count
            AS [Avg Physical Reads]
        ,qs.total_grant_kb AS [Total Grant KB]
        ,qs.last_grant_kb AS [Last Grant KB]
        ,(qs.total_grant_kb / qs.execution_count)
            AS [Avg Grant KB]
        ,qs.total_used_grant_kb AS [Total Used Grant KB]
        ,qs.last_used_grant_kb AS [Last Used Grant KB]
        ,(qs.total_used_grant_kb / qs.execution_count)
            AS [Avg Used Grant KB]
        ,qs.total_ideal_grant_kb AS [Total Ideal Grant KB]
        ,qs.last_ideal_grant_kb AS [Last Ideal Grant KB]
        ,(qs.total_ideal_grant_kb / qs.execution_count)
            AS [Avg Ideal Grant KB]
        ,qs.total_columnstore_segment_reads
            AS [Total CSI Segments Read]
        ,qs.last_columnstore_segment_reads
            AS [Last CSI Segments Read]
        ,(qs.total_columnstore_segment_reads / qs.execution_count)
            AS [AVG CSI Segments Read]
        ,qs.max_dop AS [Max DOP]
        ,qs.total_spills AS [Total Spills]
        ,qs.last_spills AS [Last Spills]
        ,(qs.total_spills / qs.execution_count) AS [Avg Spills]
        ,qs.statement_start_offset
        ,qs.statement_end_offset
        ,qs.plan_handle
        ,qs.sql_handle
    FROM
        sys.dm_exec_query_stats qs WITH (NOLOCK)
    ORDER BY
        [Avg IO] DESC
)
SELECT
    SUBSTRING(qt.text, (qs.statement_start_offset/2)+1,
    ((
        CASE qs.statement_end_offset
            WHEN -1 THEN DATALENGTH(qt.text)
            ELSE qs.statement_end_offset
        END - qs.statement_start_offset)/2)+1) AS SQL
    ,TRY_CONVERT(xml,qp.query_plan) AS [Query Plan]
    ,qs.*
FROM
    Queries qs
        OUTER APPLY sys.dm_exec_sql_text(qs.sql_handle) qt
        OUTER APPLY
            sys.dm_exec_text_query_plan
            (
                qs.plan_handle
                ,qs.statement_start_offset
                ,qs.statement_end_offset
            ) qp
OPTION (RECOMPILE, MAXDOP 1);

Sort by whatever matches your tuning goal — by I/O when you need to cut disk load, by CPU on a CPU-bound system, and so on.

A useful detail

The plans returned here carry no actual execution metrics — they're effectively estimated plans. Keep that in mind while tuning (Chapter 5).

Better plansActual plans, if you're on 2019+

In SQL Server 2019+ and Azure SQL Database, at compatibility level 150, you can collect the last actual execution plan by enabling the LAST_QUERY_PLAN_STATS database option. Overhead is small. Read it through sys.dm_exec_query_plan_stats — and you can simply swap that function in for sys.dm_exec_text_query_plan in every script in this chapter.

Two ways to fetch a plan

FunctionReturnsCatch
sys.dm_exec_query_planThe whole batch's plan as XMLInternally limited to 2 MB of XML; may return NULL for complex plans
sys.dm_exec_text_query_planText plan — whole batch or a single statement via its offsetNone of the size trouble; used in the listings

Listing 4-1 wraps the plan in TRY_CONVERT, which returns NULL when the XML exceeds 2 MB. Remove it if you need to handle big plans (or on 2005–2008R2).

LimitationsThree things that will trip you up

#LimitationWhat to do
1No cached plan = no data. Queries using statement-level recompile on ad-hoc statements, or procedures run with a RECOMPILE clause, don't get plans cached at all. Evicted plans are gone too.Caption them with the Query Store or xEvents. (Infrequent queries are rarely the first priority anyway, so this usually matters less than it sounds.)
2Cache lifetime varies by plan, which skews totals. A cheap query cached early can out-total an expensive query cached recently.Look at creation_time and last_execution_time. Then run the analysis sorted by both total and average metrics, factor in executions per second, and reconcile the two outputs before choosing.
3Duplicate rows for the same query. Happens with ad-hoc workloads, clients using different SET options, slightly different formatting, and — on compatibility level 160 (SQL Server 2022) — parameter-sensitive plan optimization.Aggregate using query_hash and query_plan_hash. Identical values mean similar queries and plans.

Note the subtle case for stored procedures: with statement-level recompile, SQL Server does cache the statement's plan — but never reuses it, so its statistics only reflect the last single execution.

Demo warning

Listing 4-2 begins with DBCC FREEPROCCACHE to keep the output small for demonstration. Never run that on production.

Listing 4-2 — The query_hash and query_plan_hash queries in actionT-SQL
DBCC FREEPROCCACHE -- Do not run in production!
GO
SELECT /*V1*/ TOP 1 object_id FROM sys.objects WHERE object_id = 1;
GO
SELECT /*V2*/ TOP 1 object_id
FROM sys.objects
WHERE object_id = 1;
GO
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM sys.objects
GO
SELECT
    qs.query_hash, qs.query_plan_hash, qs.sql_handle, qs.plan_handle,
    SUBSTRING(qt.text, (qs.statement_start_offset/2)+1,
    ((
        CASE qs.statement_end_offset
            WHEN -1 THEN DATALENGTH(qt.text)
            ELSE qs.statement_end_offset
        END - qs.statement_start_offset)/2)+1
    ) as SQL
FROM
    sys.dm_exec_query_stats qs
        CROSS APPLY sys.dm_exec_sql_text(qs.sql_handle) qt
ORDER BY query_hash
OPTION (MAXDOP 1, RECOMPILE);

The first two queries are the same query — only formatted differently (the /*V1*/ and /*V2*/ comments and the line breaks). The third is genuinely different. The output has three plans, and the last two rows share identical query_hash and query_plan_hash values but different handles:

Listing 4-3 builds the aggregation. It groups by query_hash, sums the metrics, and reports a [Plan Count]. Note the honest caveat: the SQL text and plan are picked at random from the first query in each group, so factor that in.

Listing 4-3 — sys.dm_exec_query_stats with query_hash aggregationT-SQL
;WITH Data
AS
(
    SELECT TOP 50
        qs.query_hash
        ,COUNT(*) as [Plan Count]
        ,MIN(qs.creation_time) AS [Cached Time]
        ,MAX(qs.last_execution_time) AS [Last Exec Time]
        ,SUM(qs.execution_count) AS [Exec Cnt]
        ,SUM(qs.total_logical_reads) AS [Total Reads]
        ,SUM(qs.total_logical_writes) AS [Total Writes]
        ,SUM(qs.total_worker_time / 1000) AS [Total Worker Time]
        ,SUM(qs.total_elapsed_time / 1000) AS [Total Elapsed Time]
        ,SUM(qs.total_rows) AS [Total Rows]
        ,SUM(qs.total_physical_reads) AS [Total Physical Reads]
        ,SUM(qs.total_grant_kb) AS [Total Grant KB]
        ,SUM(qs.total_used_grant_kb) AS [Total Used Grant KB]
        ,SUM(qs.total_ideal_grant_kb) AS [Total Ideal Grant KB]
        ,SUM(qs.total_columnstore_segment_reads)
            AS [Total CSI Segments Read]
        ,MAX(qs.max_dop) AS [Max DOP]
        ,SUM(qs.total_spills) AS [Total Spills]
    FROM
        sys.dm_exec_query_stats qs WITH (NOLOCK)
    GROUP BY
        qs.query_hash
    ORDER BY
        SUM((qs.total_logical_reads + qs.total_logical_writes) /
            qs.execution_count) DESC
)
SELECT
    d.[Cached Time]
    ,d.[Last Exec Time]
    ,d.[Plan Count]
    ,sql_plan.SQL
    ,sql_plan.[Query Plan]
    ,d.[Exec Cnt]
    ,CONVERT(DECIMAL(10,5),
        IIF(datediff(second,d.[Cached Time], d.[Last Exec Time]) = 0,
            NULL,
            1.0 * d.[Exec Cnt] /
                datediff(second,d.[Cached Time], d.[Last Exec Time])
        )
    ) AS [Exec Per Second]
    ,(d.[Total Reads] + d.[Total Writes]) / d.[Exec Cnt] AS [Avg IO]
    ,(d.[Total Worker Time] / d.[Exec Cnt] / 1000) AS [Avg CPU(ms)]
    ,d.[Total Reads]
    ,d.[Total Writes]
    ,d.[Total Worker Time]
    ,d.[Total Elapsed Time]
    ,d.[Total Rows]
    ,d.[Total Rows] / d.[Exec Cnt] AS [Avg Rows]
    ,d.[Total Physical Reads]
    ,d.[Total Physical Reads] / d.[Exec Cnt] AS [Avg Physical Reads]
    ,d.[Total Grant KB]
    ,d.[Total Grant KB] / d.[Exec Cnt] AS [Avg Grant KB]
    ,d.[Total Used Grant KB]
    ,d.[Total Used Grant KB] / d.[Exec Cnt] AS [Avg Used Grant KB]
    ,d.[Total Ideal Grant KB]
    ,d.[Total Ideal Grant KB] / d.[Exec Cnt] AS [Avg Ideal Grant KB]
    ,d.[Total CSI Segments Read]
    ,d.[Total CSI Segments Read] / d.[Exec Cnt] AS [AVG CSI Segments Read]
    ,d.[Max DOP]
    ,d.[Total Spills]
    ,d.[Total Spills] / d.[Exec Cnt] AS [Avg Spills]
FROM
    Data d
        CROSS APPLY
        (
            SELECT TOP 1
                SUBSTRING(qt.text, (qs.statement_start_offset/2)+1,
                ((
                    CASE qs.statement_end_offset
                        WHEN -1 THEN DATALENGTH(qt.text)
                        ELSE qs.statement_end_offset
                    END - qs.statement_start_offset)/2)+1
                ) AS SQL
                ,TRY_CONVERT(XML,qp.query_plan) AS [Query Plan]
            FROM
                sys.dm_exec_query_stats qs
                    OUTER APPLY sys.dm_exec_sql_text(qs.sql_handle) qt
                    OUTER APPLY sys.dm_exec_text_query_plan
                    (
                        qs.plan_handle
                        ,qs.statement_start_offset
                        ,qs.statement_end_offset
                    ) qp
            WHERE
                qs.query_hash = d.query_hash AND ISNULL(qt.text,'') <> ''
        ) sql_plan
ORDER BY
     [Avg IO] DESC
OPTION (RECOMPILE, MAXDOP 1);

Same idea, other objectsProcedures, triggers, functions

Since SQL Server 2008, sys.dm_exec_procedure_stats gives you the same treatment for stored procedures:

Listing 4-4 — Using the sys.dm_exec_procedure_stats viewT-SQL
SELECT TOP 50
    IIF (ps.database_id = 32767,
         'mssqlsystemresource',
         DB_NAME(ps.database_id)
    ) AS [DB]
    ,OBJECT_NAME(
         ps.object_id,
         IIF(ps.database_id = 32767, 1, ps.database_id)
    ) AS [Proc Name]
    ,ps.type_desc AS [Type]
    ,ps.cached_time AS [Cached Time]
    ,ps.last_execution_time AS [Last Exec Time]
    ,qp.query_plan AS [Plan]
    ,ps.execution_count AS [Exec Count]
    ,CONVERT(DECIMAL(10,5),
        IIF(datediff(second,ps.cached_time, ps.last_execution_time) = 0,
            NULL,
            1.0 * ps.execution_count /
                datediff(second,ps.cached_time, ps.last_execution_time)
        )
    ) AS [Exec Per Second]
    ,(ps.total_logical_reads + ps.total_logical_writes) /
        ps.execution_count AS [Avg IO]
    ,(ps.total_worker_time / ps.execution_count / 1000)
        AS [Avg CPU(ms)]
    ,ps.total_logical_reads AS [Total Reads]
    ,ps.last_logical_reads AS [Last Reads]
    ,ps.total_logical_writes AS [Total Writes]
    ,ps.last_logical_writes AS [Last Writes]
    ,ps.total_worker_time / 1000 AS [Total Worker Time]
    ,ps.last_worker_time / 1000 AS [Last Worker Time]
    ,ps.total_elapsed_time / 1000 AS [Total Elapsed Time]
    ,ps.last_elapsed_time / 1000 AS [Last Elapsed Time]
    ,ps.total_physical_reads AS [Total Physical Reads]
    ,ps.last_physical_reads AS [Last Physical Reads]
    ,ps.total_physical_reads / ps.execution_count AS [Avg Physical Reads]
    ,ps.total_spills AS [Total Spills]
    ,ps.last_spills AS [Last Spills]
    ,(ps.total_spills / ps.execution_count) AS [Avg Spills]
FROM
    sys.dm_exec_procedure_stats ps WITH (NOLOCK)
        CROSS APPLY sys.dm_exec_query_plan(ps.plan_handle) qp
ORDER BY
     [Avg IO] DESC
OPTION (RECOMPILE, MAXDOP 1);

Two things worth knowing. First, the statistics include metrics from dynamic SQL and from nested modules (other procedures, functions, triggers) called by the procedure. Second, a procedure's plan is really just a collection of each statement's individual plan — and when a plan exceeds 2 MB, the [Plan] column comes back empty:

When you hit a NULL plan, Listing 4-5 gets you the individual statements inside a module. Just fill in the procedure name in the WHERE clause:

Listing 4-5 — Getting the execution plan and statistics for stored procedure statementsT-SQL
SELECT
    qs.creation_time AS [Cached Time]
    ,qs.last_execution_time AS [Last Exec Time]
    ,SUBSTRING(qt.text, (qs.statement_start_offset/2)+1,
    ((
        CASE qs.statement_end_offset
            WHEN -1 THEN DATALENGTH(qt.text)
            ELSE qs.statement_end_offset
        END - qs.statement_start_offset)/2)+1) AS SQL
    ,TRY_CONVERT(XML,qp.query_plan) AS [Query Plan]
    ,CONVERT(DECIMAL(10,5),
        IIF(datediff(second,qs.creation_time, qs.last_execution_time) = 0,
            NULL,
            1.0 * qs.execution_count /
                datediff(second,qs.creation_time, qs.last_execution_time)
        )
    ) AS [Exec Per Second]
    ,(qs.total_logical_reads + qs.total_logical_writes) /
        qs.execution_count AS [Avg IO]
    ,(qs.total_worker_time / qs.execution_count / 1000)
        AS [Avg CPU(ms)]
    ,qs.total_logical_reads AS [Total Reads]
    ,qs.last_logical_reads AS [Last Reads]
    ,qs.total_logical_writes AS [Total Writes]
    ,qs.last_logical_writes AS [Last Writes]
    ,qs.total_worker_time / 1000 AS [Total Worker Time]
    ,qs.last_worker_time / 1000 AS [Last Worker Time]
    ,qs.total_elapsed_time / 1000 AS [Total Elapsed Time]
    ,qs.last_elapsed_time / 1000 AS [Last Elapsed Time]
    ,qs.total_rows AS [Total Rows]
    ,qs.last_rows AS [Last Rows]
    ,qs.total_rows / qs.execution_count AS [Avg Rows]
    ,qs.total_physical_reads AS [Total Physical Reads]
    ,qs.last_physical_reads AS [Last Physical Reads]
    ,qs.total_physical_reads / qs.execution_count
        AS [Avg Physical Reads]
    ,qs.total_grant_kb AS [Total Grant KB]
    ,qs.last_grant_kb AS [Last Grant KB]
    ,(qs.total_grant_kb / qs.execution_count)
        AS [Avg Grant KB]
    ,qs.total_used_grant_kb AS [Total Used Grant KB]
    ,qs.last_used_grant_kb AS [Last Used Grant KB]
    ,(qs.total_used_grant_kb / qs.execution_count)
        AS [Avg Used Grant KB]
    ,qs.total_ideal_grant_kb AS [Total Ideal Grant KB]
    ,qs.last_ideal_grant_kb AS [Last Ideal Grant KB]
    ,(qs.total_ideal_grant_kb / qs.execution_count)
        AS [Avg Ideal Grant KB]
    ,qs.total_columnstore_segment_reads
        AS [Total CSI Segments Read]
    ,qs.last_columnstore_segment_reads
        AS [Last CSI Segments Read]
    ,(qs.total_columnstore_segment_reads / qs.execution_count)
        AS [AVG CSI Segments Read]
    ,qs.max_dop AS [Max DOP]
    ,qs.total_spills AS [Total Spills]
    ,qs.last_spills AS [Last Spills]
    ,(qs.total_spills / qs.execution_count) AS [Avg Spills]
FROM
    sys.dm_exec_query_stats qs WITH (NOLOCK)
        OUTER APPLY sys.dm_exec_sql_text(qs.sql_handle) qt
        OUTER APPLY sys.dm_exec_text_query_plan
        (
            qs.plan_handle
            ,qs.statement_start_offset
            ,qs.statement_end_offset
        ) qp
WHERE
    OBJECT_NAME(qt.objectid, qt.dbid) = <SP Name> -- Add SP Name here
ORDER BY
    qs.statement_start_offset, qs.statement_end_offset
OPTION (RECOMPILE, MAXDOP 1);

Since SQL Server 2016 the same pattern covers triggers and scalar UDFs via sys.dm_exec_trigger_stats and sys.dm_exec_function_stats — just swap the view name in Listing 4-4.

Practical caution

SQL Server may cache thousands of plans, and the functions that fetch plans and SQL text are resource intensive — hence the MAXDOP 1 hint used to limit overhead. On a busy server, consider dumping the plan cache into a separate database with SELECT INTO and analysing it on a non-production machine.

Why start here anyway

You'll miss some queries. But the data is collected automatically and available immediately, with zero monitoring to set up. That makes it a genuinely great starting point.

3Extended Events and SQL Traces

Both technologies capture events in real time, so you can catch long-running and expensive queries — including the ones that never cache a plan and therefore never show up in sys.dm_exec_query_stats.

Read this before you build a session

Don't use SQL Traces or xEvents for this unless it's absolutely necessary. Capturing executed statements is expensive and can add serious overhead on busy systems — you saw a live example back in Chapter 1, where one session cost ~20% of throughput.

And filtering doesn't save you: it doesn't matter how much data you keep. SQL Server still has to capture every statement first in order to evaluate, filter, and discard.

Two more rules: don't collect unnecessary actions — some, like callstack, are expensive and can cause a serious hit — and prefer xEvents over SQL Traces, since they're lighter and introduce less overhead.

Event referenceWhat to capture

xEventSQL Trace eventFires / notes
sqlserver.sql_statement_completedSQL:StmtCompletedStatement finished. Catches inefficient ad-hoc queries.
sqlserver.sp_statement_completedSP:StmtCompletedStatement inside a T-SQL module finished.
sqlserver.rpc_completedRPC:CompletedRemote procedure call completed. RPCs are parameterized requests — stored procedure calls or parameterized batches. Many client libraries run queries via sp_executesql, so this catches a lot.
sqlserver.module_endSP:CompletedT-SQL module finished.
sqlserver.sql_batch_completedSQL:BatchCompletedBatch finished.
sqlserver.attentionError:AttentionClient cancelled the query — a timeout, or the red cancel button in SSMS.

Pick based on workload and strategy. Capturing sql_statement_completed and sp_statement_completed gives you fine-grained detection of ad-hoc and module queries. Capturing rpc_completed and sql_batch_completed instead sees whole batches and procedures with lower overhead — a reasonable trade.

Same logic for actions: skip user and client-application details if you don't need them, or do collect query_hash and query_plan_hash so you can aggregate the cumulative impact of similar queries.

Two ways to run it

StyleTargetWhen
Short burst — a few minutesring_bufferWorkload is relatively static and a small sample represents it
Long run — a few hoursevent_fileYou need to catch intermittent expensive queries

Listing 4-6 is the second style. It captures statements consuming more than 5,000 ms of CPU, more than 50,000 logical reads, or more than 50,000 writes, writing to C:\ExtEvents. Works on SQL Server 2012+; 2008 needs modification (different file-target behaviour, no query_hash/query_plan_hash actions).

Listing 4-6 — Capturing CPU- and I/O-intensive queriesT-SQL
CREATE EVENT SESSION [Expensive Queries]
ON SERVER
ADD EVENT sqlserver.sql_statement_completed
(
    ACTION
    (
        sqlserver.client_app_name
        ,sqlserver.client_hostname
        ,sqlserver.database_id
        ,sqlserver.plan_handle
        ,sqlserver.query_hash
        ,sqlserver.query_plan_hash
        ,sqlserver.sql_text
        ,sqlserver.username
    )
    WHERE
    (
        (
            cpu_time >= 5000000 or -- Time in microseconds
            logical_reads >= 50000 or
            writes >= 50000
        ) AND
        sqlserver.is_system = 0
    )
)
,ADD EVENT sqlserver.sp_statement_completed
(
    ACTION
    (
        sqlserver.client_app_name
        ,sqlserver.client_hostname
        ,sqlserver.database_id
        ,sqlserver.plan_handle
        ,sqlserver.query_hash
        ,sqlserver.query_plan_hash
        ,sqlserver.sql_text
        ,sqlserver.username
    )
    WHERE
    (
        (
            cpu_time >= 5000000 or -- Time in microseconds
            logical_reads >= 50000 or
            writes >= 50000
        ) AND
        sqlserver.is_system = 0
    )
)
ADD TARGET package0.event_file
(
    SET FILENAME = 'C:\ExtEvents\Expensive Queries.xel'
)
WITH
(
    event_retention_mode=allow_single_event_loss
    ,max_dispatch_latency=30 seconds
);
Tune it to your workload

This session does add overhead, proportional to workload and capture volume. Don't leave it running unless you're actively troubleshooting. Adjust the cpu_time, logical_reads, and writes thresholds to your system, and resist capturing excessive numbers of queries. Also drop actions you won't use — there's no point collecting plan_handle if you'll analyse the data on another server and can't reach this one's plan cache.

Listing 4-7 parses the output. It first loads the events into a temp table via sys.fn_xe_file_target_read_file — the asterisk in the filename loads all rollover files — then shreds the XML into typed columns. Only parse what you need; shredding XML is expensive and slow.

Version note: on SQL Server 2017+ the function returns timestamp_utc directly. On 2016 and earlier you must pull the time out of the event_data XML instead (the commented-out alternative in the code).

Listing 4-7 — Parsing collected xEvent dataT-SQL
CREATE TABLE #EventData
(
  event_data XML NOT NULL,
  file_name NVARCHAR(260) NOT NULL,
  file_offset BIGINT NOT NULL,
  timestamp_utc datetime2(7) NOT NULL -- SQL Server 2017+
);
INSERT INTO #EventData(event_data, file_name, file_offset, timestamp_utc)
  SELECT CONVERT(XML,event_data), file_name, file_offset, timestamp_utc
  FROM sys.fn_xe_file_target_read_file
    ('c:\extevents\Expensive Queries*.xel',NULL,NULL,NULL);

;WITH EventInfo([Event],[Event Time],[DB],[Statement],[SQL],[User Name]
  ,[Client],[App],[CPU Time],[Duration],[Logical Reads]
  ,[Physical Reads],[Writes],[Rows],[Query Hash],[Plan Hash]
  ,[PlanHandle],[Stmt Offset],[Stmt Offset End],File_Name,File_Offset)
AS
(
  SELECT
    event_data.value('/event[1]/@name','SYSNAME') AS [Event]
    ,timestamp_utc AS [Event Time] -- SQL Server 2017+
    /*,event_data.value('/event[1]/@timestamp','DATETIME')
        AS [Event Time] -- Prior SQL Server 2017 */
    ,event_data.value
       ('((/event[1]/action[@name="database_id"]/value/text())[1])'
         ,'INT') AS [DB]
    ,event_data.value
       ('((/event[1]/data[@name="statement"]/value/text())[1])'
         ,'NVARCHAR(MAX)') AS [Statement]
    ,event_data.value
       ('((/event[1]/action[@name="sql_text"]/value/text())[1])'
         ,'NVARCHAR(MAX)') AS [SQL]
    ,event_data.value
       ('((/event[1]/action[@name="username"]/value/text())[1])'
         ,'NVARCHAR(255)') AS [User Name]
    ,event_data.value
       ('((/event[1]/action[@name="client_hostname"]/value/text())[1])'
         ,'NVARCHAR(255)') AS [Client]
    ,event_data.value
       ('((/event[1]/action[@name="client_app_name"]/value/text())[1])'
         ,'NVARCHAR(255)') AS [App]
    ,event_data.value
       ('((/event[1]/data[@name="cpu_time"]/value/text())[1])'
         ,'BIGINT') AS [CPU Time]
    ,event_data.value
       ('((/event[1]/data[@name="duration"]/value/text())[1])'
         ,'BIGINT') AS [Duration]
    ,event_data.value
       ('((/event[1]/data[@name="logical_reads"]/value/text())[1])'
         ,'INT') AS [Logical Reads]
    ,event_data.value
       ('((/event[1]/data[@name="physical_reads"]/value/text())[1])'
         ,'INT') AS [Physical Reads]
    ,event_data.value
       ('((/event[1]/data[@name="writes"]/value/text())[1])'
         ,'INT') AS [Writes]
    ,event_data.value
       ('((/event[1]/data[@name="row_count"]/value/text())[1])'
         ,'INT') AS [Rows]
    ,event_data.value(
       'xs:hexBinary(((/event[1]/action[@name="query_hash"]/value/text())[1]))'
         ,'BINARY(8)') AS [Query Hash]
    ,event_data.value(
      'xs:hexBinary(((/event[1]/action[@name="query_plan_hash"]/value/text())[1]))'
         ,'BINARY(8)') AS [Plan Hash]
    ,event_data.value(
      'xs:hexBinary(((/event[1]/action[@name="plan_handle"]/value/text())[1]))'
         ,'VARBINARY(64)') AS [PlanHandle]
    ,event_data.value
      ('((/event[1]/data[@name="offset"]/value/text())[1])'
         ,'INT') AS [Stmt Offset]
    ,event_data.value
       ('((/event[1]/data[@name="offset_end"]/value/text())[1])'
         ,'INT') AS [Stmt Offset End]
    ,file_name
    ,file_offset
  FROM
    #EventData
)
SELECT
  ei.*
  ,TRY_CONVERT(XML,qp.Query_Plan) AS [Plan]
INTO #Queries
FROM
  EventInfo ei
    OUTER APPLY
      sys.dm_exec_text_query_plan
      (
        ei.PlanHandle
        ,ei.[Stmt Offset]
        ,ei.[Stmt Offset End]
      ) qp
OPTION (MAXDOP 1, RECOMPILE);

Then work the #Queries table directly — and usually aggregate by statement, query hash, or plan hash to see cumulative impact rather than individual outliers.

The ring_buffer gotcha

sys.dm_xe_session_targets can only output 4 MB of XML. With a ring_buffer target you may silently lose collected events. Another argument for short sessions.

And the recurring warning: do not create these sessions permanently. A few minutes is usually enough to gather what you need.

4Query Store

Both previous approaches have problems. Plan cache data misses queries; xEvents and traces demand complex post-processing and carry real overhead. The Query Store (SQL Server 2016+) addresses exactly those gaps.

The best analogy in the book

The Query Store is SQL Server's flight data recorder — its black box. It captures and persists runtime statistics and execution plans per database, shows how plans perform and how they evolve over time, and lets you force a specific plan onto a query to fix parameter-sniffing problems (Chapter 6).

Is it on?

Disabled by default on-premises up to SQL Server 2019. Enabled by default in Azure SQL Database, Azure SQL Managed Instance, and new databases in SQL Server 2022.

IntegrationWhere it sits in the pipeline

The Query Store is fully integrated into query processing, not bolted on the side:

  • On a plan-cache hit, SQL Server checks whether the query needs recompiling (statistics updates, schema changes, a newly forced or unforced plan) and whether an old forced plan has been dropped from the store.
  • During compilation it checks for an available forced plan and compiles with it — much like the USE PLAN hint. If the resulting plan is valid, it lands in the plan cache for reuse.
  • If the forced plan is no longer valid (say a user dropped an index it referenced), the query does not fail. SQL Server recompiles without the forced plan and doesn't cache it. The Query Store persists both plans and marks the forced one invalid — all transparently to the application.

In SQL Server 2022 and Azure SQL Database, sp_query_store_set_hints lets you attach query-level hints. SQL Server then compiles and executes as if you'd written an OPTION clause — extra tuning flexibility without touching application code.

CostWhat drives the overhead

FactorWhy
Number of compilationsEvery compilation is load for the Query Store. Very heavy ad-hoc, nonparameterized workloads are its weak spot.
Collection settingsCapture everything vs. only expensive queries; smaller aggregation intervals and longer retention both mean more data and more overhead.

QUERY_CAPTURE_MODE is the setting to watch:

ModeBehaviourVerdict
ALLDefault in 2016/2017 — captures every queryRisky on ad-hoc workloads
AUTODefault in 2019+ — skips small and infrequently executed queriesBest option in most cases
CUSTOM2019+ — define your own capture criteriaFine-grained control
A real 3× slowdown

The author used the Query Store on a process made of a very large number of small ad-hoc queries, with QUERY_CAPTURE_MODE=ALL. It collected almost 10 GB of Query Store data. With the Query Store enabled the process took 8 hours; without it, 2.5 hours. Configuration is everything.

Properly configured, overhead is usually small — and the author still recommends enabling it, because some Intelligent Query Processing (IQP) features depend on the Query Store, and it simplifies tuning enough to save many hours.

Monitor QDS* waits once enabled; excessive values suggest higher overhead. Ignore QDS_PERSIST_TASK_MAIN_LOOP_SLEEP and QDS_ASYNC_QUEUE — they're benign.

Two trace flagsWorth knowing

FlagProblem it solves
T7745SQL Server caches Query Store data in memory and flushes periodically (DATA_FLUSH_INTERVAL_SECONDS controls how much you lose in a crash). Normally it flushes in-memory data on shutdown or failover too — which can prolong shutdown and failover on busy systems. This flag disables that; losing a little telemetry is usually acceptable.
T7752
(2016/2017)		SQL Server loads Query Store data into memory at database startup, keeping the database unavailable meanwhile. Large stores mean slow restart/failover. This flag loads asynchronously so queries can run in parallel — no telemetry during the load, which is a fair trade. Measure the impact by looking at QDS_LOADDB wait time (startup only).

General rules: don't create a very large Query Store, monitor its size in busy systems (cleanup may not keep up, especially with QUERY_CAPTURE_MODE=ALL), and apply the latest updates — many scalability fixes and bug fixes for this feature shipped after release, particularly for 2016/2017.

Option AThe SSMS reports

Once enabled, a Query Store folder appears in Object Explorer. The exact report list depends on your SQL Server and SSMS versions; the book walks through seven.

ReportWhat it's for
Regressed QueriesQueries whose performance got worse over time. Configurable timeframe and regression criteria (disk ops, CPU, execution count). Pick a query in the upper-left graph; upper-right shows its collected plans as dots — click one to see the plan below and compare plans. The Force Plan / Unforce Plan buttons call sp_query_store_force_plan / ..._unforce_plan. Best tool for parameter sniffing issues.
Top Resource Consuming QueriesThe Query Store equivalent of sys.dm_exec_query_stats — but without depending on the plan cache. Customisable metric and time interval.
Overall Resource ConsumptionWorkload statistics and resource usage per interval — spots spikes and drills into the queries that caused them.
Queries With High VariationPinpoints queries with unstable performance — anomalies and possible regressions.
Queries With Forced PlansEverything currently forced in the system.
Query Wait StatisticsQueries with high waits, grouped into categories (CPU, disk, blocking).
Tracked QueriesMonitor plans and statistics for individual queries — same info as Regressed/Top Consumers, scoped to one query.

Option BQuery Store DMVs

The DMVs are highly normalized. Runtime statistics are tracked per plan and grouped into collection intervals set by INTERVAL_LENGTH_MINUTES — default 60 minutes, which is fine for most cases. Smaller intervals mean more data persisted; a huge ad-hoc workload can balloon the store.

GroupViewContains
Plan storesys.query_store_queryQueries, compilation statistics, last execution time
sys.query_store_query_textThe query text
sys.query_context_settingContext settings: SET options, default schema, language. Different settings can mean separate cached plans for the same query.
sys.query_store_planExecution plans. is_forced_plan flags a forced plan; last_force_failure_reason explains why a forced plan wasn't applied.
Runtime statssys.query_store_runtime_stats_intervalCollection intervals
sys.query_store_runtime_statsPer-plan stats for one interval: execution count, CPU, duration, logical and physical I/O, log usage, DOP, memory grant size, and more
sys.query_store_wait_stats
(2017+)		Waits per plan per interval, grouped into categories (CPU, memory, blocking)

Because a query can have several rows in query and plan (context settings, recompilations), you must aggregate across intervals to get meaningful numbers.

Listing 4-8 answers "what are my 50 most I/O-intensive queries". Because stats persist per interval, it multiplies count_executions by each avg_* column and sums — then divides by total executions to get a true weighted average. Note the Query Store uses datetimeoffset for dates, so filter with SYSDATETIMEOFFSET():

Listing 4-8 — Getting information about expensive queries from the Query StoreT-SQL
SELECT TOP 50
  q.query_id, qt.query_sql_text, qp.plan_id, qp.query_plan
  ,SUM(rs.count_executions) AS [Execution Cnt]
  ,CONVERT(INT,SUM(rs.count_executions *
    (rs.avg_logical_io_reads + avg_logical_io_writes)) /
      SUM(rs.count_executions)) AS [Avg IO]
  ,CONVERT(INT,SUM(rs.count_executions *
    (rs.avg_logical_io_reads + avg_logical_io_writes))) AS [Total IO]
  ,CONVERT(INT,SUM(rs.count_executions * rs.avg_cpu_time) /
    SUM(rs.count_executions)) AS [Avg CPU]
  ,CONVERT(INT,SUM(rs.count_executions * rs.avg_cpu_time)) AS [Total CPU]
  ,CONVERT(INT,SUM(rs.count_executions * rs.avg_duration) /
    SUM(rs.count_executions)) AS [Avg Duration]
  ,CONVERT(INT,SUM(rs.count_executions * rs.avg_duration))
    AS [Total Duration]
  ,CONVERT(INT,SUM(rs.count_executions * rs.avg_physical_io_reads) /
    SUM(rs.count_executions)) AS [Avg Physical Reads]
  ,CONVERT(INT,SUM(rs.count_executions * rs.avg_physical_io_reads))
    AS [Total Physical Reads]
  ,CONVERT(INT,SUM(rs.count_executions * rs.avg_query_max_used_memory) /
    SUM(rs.count_executions)) AS [Avg Memory Grant Pages]
  ,CONVERT(INT,SUM(rs.count_executions * rs.avg_query_max_used_memory))
    AS [Total Memory Grant Pages]
  ,CONVERT(INT,SUM(rs.count_executions * rs.avg_rowcount) /
    SUM(rs.count_executions)) AS [Avg Rows]
  ,CONVERT(INT,SUM(rs.count_executions * rs.avg_rowcount)) AS [Total Rows]
  ,CONVERT(INT,SUM(rs.count_executions * rs.avg_dop) /
    SUM(rs.count_executions)) AS [Avg DOP]
  ,CONVERT(INT,SUM(rs.count_executions * rs.avg_dop)) AS [Total DOP]
FROM
  sys.query_store_query q WITH (NOLOCK)
    JOIN sys.query_store_plan qp WITH (NOLOCK) ON
      q.query_id = qp.query_id
    JOIN sys.query_store_query_text qt WITH (NOLOCK) ON
      q.query_text_id = qt.query_text_id
    JOIN sys.query_store_runtime_stats rs WITH (NOLOCK) ON
      qp.plan_id = rs.plan_id
    JOIN sys.query_store_runtime_stats_interval rsi WITH (NOLOCK) ON
      rs.runtime_stats_interval_id = rsi.runtime_stats_interval_id
WHERE
  rsi.end_time >= DATEADD(DAY,-1,SYSDATETIMEOFFSET())
GROUP BY
  q.query_id, qt.query_sql_text, qp.plan_id, qp.query_plan
ORDER BY
  [Avg IO] DESC
OPTION (MAXDOP 1, RECOMPILE);

Sort by anything you like, and add predicates to narrow results. Two neat examples the book suggests: filter by the DOP columns to find queries going parallel in an OLTP system (and fine-tune Cost Threshold for Parallelism), or hunt down queries that balloon the plan cache.

Listing 4-9 finds queries generating multiple plans from different context settings. The two usual culprits: sessions using different SET options, and queries referencing objects without schema names.

Listing 4-9 — Queries with different context settingsT-SQL
SELECT
    q.query_id, qt.query_sql_text
    ,COUNT(DISTINCT q.context_settings_id) AS [Context Setting Cnt]
    ,COUNT(DISTINCT qp.plan_id) AS [Plan Count]
FROM
    sys.query_store_query q WITH (NOLOCK)
        JOIN sys.query_store_query_text qt WITH (NOLOCK) ON
            q.query_text_id = qt.query_text_id
        JOIN sys.query_store_plan qp WITH (NOLOCK) ON
            q.query_id = qp.query_id
GROUP BY
    q.query_id, qt.query_sql_text
HAVING
    COUNT(DISTINCT q.context_settings_id) > 1
ORDER BY
    COUNT(DISTINCT q.context_settings_id)
OPTION (MAXDOP 1, RECOMPILE);

Listing 4-10 finds similar queries by query_hash — typically a nonparameterized ad-hoc workload. Fix it by parameterizing in code; if that's impossible, consider forced parameterization (Chapter 6). The output shows one randomly chosen query per group as a sample.

Listing 4-10 — Detecting queries with duplicated query_hash valuesT-SQL
;WITH Queries(query_hash, [Query Count], [Exec Count], qtid)
AS
(
    SELECT TOP 100
        q.query_hash
        ,COUNT(DISTINCT q.query_id)
        ,SUM(rs.count_executions)
        ,MIN(q.query_text_id)
    FROM
        sys.query_store_query q WITH (NOLOCK)
            JOIN sys.query_store_plan qp WITH (NOLOCK) ON
                q.query_id = qp.query_id
            JOIN sys.query_store_runtime_stats rs WITH (NOLOCK) ON
                qp.plan_id = rs.plan_id
    GROUP BY
        q.query_hash
    HAVING
        COUNT(DISTINCT q.query_id) > 1
)
SELECT
    q.query_hash
    ,qt.query_sql_text AS [Sample SQL]
    ,q.[Query Count]
    ,q.[Exec Count]
FROM
    Queries q CROSS APPLY
    (
        SELECT TOP 1 qt.query_sql_text
        FROM sys.query_store_query_text qt WITH (NOLOCK)
        WHERE qt.query_text_id = q.qtid
    ) qt
ORDER BY
    [Query Count] DESC, [Exec Count] DESC
OPTION(MAXDOP 1, RECOMPILE);
Nice trick

DBCC CLONEDATABASE produces a schema-only clone that includes Query Store data by default. Restore it elsewhere and analyse there — production overhead drops to zero.

5Third-party tools

SQL Server's built-in toolset is already rich. But vendor tools can add value: most list your most resource-intensive queries, and many provide a baseline so you can spot trends and catch regressions.

Rather than recommending products, the book offers guidance on choosing and using them:

RuleWhy it matters
Understand how it worksIf a tool polls sys.dm_exec_requests on a schedule, it will miss small-but-frequent queries that run between polls. If it infers from session waits, results depend heavily on workload and how much data is cached.
Estimate its overheadSome DMVs are very expensive. A tool calling sys.dm_exec_query_plan on every poll can measurably hurt a busy server. Tools also commonly create traces and xEvent sessions without telling you.
Don't trust "harmless"Vendor whitepapers can't account for your workload. Baseline the system with and without the tool — and remember overhead isn't static; it grows as workload changes.
Mind the security surfaceMany tools let you build custom monitors that execute queries — a door to malicious activity. Don't over-grant the tool's login, and control who can administer it.
Use them together

You don't need to optimize every inefficient query — Pareto again. But multiple perspectives help: it's trivially easy to cross-check a tool's list against plan cache–based statistics to build a more complete picture.

6Key takeaways

Inefficient queries overload the disk subsystem, but even when data is fully cached they burn CPU, increase blocking, and hurt the customer experience.

TechniqueStrengthWeakness
Plan cache
sys.dm_exec_query_stats		Instant, free, every version, no setup. Also covers procs, triggers, scalar UDFs via dm_exec_procedure_stats, dm_exec_trigger_stats, dm_exec_function_statsNo runtime metrics in plans; misses uncached queries (RECOMPILE, ad-hoc statement recompile, evictions); skewed by cache lifetime; duplicate rows — aggregate on query_hash
xEvents / SQL TracesReal-time capture, catches what the plan cache missesOverhead even when filtering; raw data needing aggregation; 4 MB ring_buffer limit. Prefer xEvents over Traces.
Query Store
(2016+)		Persists plans and stats, independent of the plan cache, spotlights plan regressions, lets you force plans. Great tool.Adds overhead — watch QUERY_CAPTURE_MODE and QDS* waits. Can be severe on huge ad-hoc workloads.
Third-party toolsConvenience, baselines, trendsUnknown blind spots and hidden overhead — research and baseline them
